hero.title: Paper Review System
hero.subtitle: Automatically finding logical-structural defects in academic papers with a Knowledge Graph + LLM
hero.lead: Upload a paper → extract the four-layer structure (EDU / Entity / RST / FRU) and write it into a Neo4j Knowledge Graph → check it with 13 REL rules (Cypher finds candidates + LLM adjudicates) → output logical defects and revision suggestions. Paired with a Human-as-judge annotation interface, a human inspects each defect one by one and quantifies the system's precision.

intro.p1: Academic paper drafts commonly have three kinds of "structural" problems: (1) claims without evidence, (2) lack of motivation, (3) cross-section disconnects. Traditionally these are caught by manual review — slow and subjective. This system aims to make that process automated, reproducible, and traceable.
intro.compareHeading: How is this different from just asking ChatGPT to revise your paper?

maintainable.ours: Rules written in YAML, editable by the advisor

arch.p1: Decoupled frontend/backend + three-tier storage. The frontend is Next.js 16 + Tailwind + shadcn/ui, the backend is FastAPI; Neo4j stores the KG (for Cypher queries), SQLite stores metadata/analysis results/cost log/human judgments, and local disk stores the original PDF files.

pipeline.p1: Analysis time is mostly spent on ~30–40 LLM calls. Most of these calls are independent of each other, so they are dispatched in parallel via a thread pool (up to 6 by default, tunable via {maxWorkers}), compressing the originally ~9-minute serial analysis to about 1/3. Text extraction and analysis both run in background tasks, the upload request returns a {jobId} immediately, and the frontend then polls for progress. A SHA-256 hash cache hit returns instantly.

kg.p1: The KG is the core of this system — the 13 rules are essentially all graph pattern matching. Five node types represent the paper's structure at different levels, strung together by six edge types.

nodes.paper: The paper itself. All other nodes point back to it via paper_id.
nodes.edu: Elementary Discourse Unit, the smallest propositional unit. Each EDU carries page+bbox coordinates — this is the foundation that lets PDF highlighting locate sentences precisely.
nodes.entity: A conceptual entity in the paper (e.g. Transformer, BLEU, WMT), split into 8 types (Concept / Method / Metric / Dataset / Model / Task / Claim / Other).
nodes.fru: Functional Rhetorical Unit, grouping consecutive EDUs into a rhetorical functional unit. 15 functions: Motivation / Claim / Evidence / Background / Definition / MethodStep / Observation / Attribution / Concession / ...
nodes.rst: Rhetorical relations from Rhetorical Structure Theory, marking nucleus-satellite. 15 types: Elaboration / Cause / Result / Contrast / Concession / Evidence / Justify / ...

kg.edgesDiagramCaption: Figure 4-1: KG schema — five node types and how the edges connect them
kg.edgesTableHeading: Meaning of the 6 edges + Vaswani examples

hasEdu.exampleSuffix: ) HAS_EDU EDU(“We propose a new simple network architecture, the Transformer”)

covers.meaning: "This rhetorical functional unit covers this small proposition"
covers.example: FRU(function=Claim) COVERS EDU(“We propose the Transformer”) — this FRU classifies the sentence as a claim

nucleus.meaning: "The core sentence of this rhetorical relation is this one (the lead)"
nucleus.example: RST(rst_type=Contrast) NUCLEUS EDU(“We propose the Transformer”) — the "new method" side of the contrast relation

satellite.meaning: "The subordinate sentence of this rhetorical relation is this one (the supporting role)"
satellite.example: Same RST(Contrast) SATELLITE EDU(“Existing models are based on RNN/CNN”) — the "old method" side of the contrast relation

er.meaning: "There is a relation between two concepts (the verb is written on the edge property predicate)"

mentionedIn.meaning: "This concept is mentioned in this small proposition"
mentionedIn.example: Entity(BLEU) MENTIONED_IN EDU(“achieves 28.4 BLEU on WMT 2014”)

kg.fruHeading: FRU's 15 functions (key — this is the main thing rule checking looks at)
kg.fruIntro: A FRU groups several consecutive EDUs into a "rhetorical functional unit". The 15 functions are the rhetorical roles common in paper writing.
kg.rstIntro: RST (Rhetorical Structure Theory) marks the rhetorical relation between two EDUs, split into nucleus (the lead) and satellite (the supporting role). The 15 types cover the inter-sentence logic common in papers.
kg.whyHeading: Why four-layer extraction (EDU / ER / FRU / RST)
kg.whyIntro: Different rules need evidence from different layers:

why.rel01: needs the FRU layer to tell which EDUs are Claims and which are Evidence
why.entity: needs Entity + ER triples to track the same concept appearing across paragraphs

Motivation.meaning: Motivation — explains why this problem matters and why the research is being done
Motivation.example: “The fundamental constraint of sequential computation, however, remains.” (Intro p.2 — explains why a new architecture is needed)

Claim.meaning: Claim — the core argument or conclusion the authors put forward
Claim.example: “We propose a new simple network architecture, the Transformer, based solely on attention mechanisms” (Abstract)

Evidence.meaning: Evidence — quantitative data, citations, or experimental results that support a claim
Evidence.example: “Our model achieves 28.4 BLEU on the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task, improving over the existing best results, including ensembles, by over 2 BLEU.” (Abstract)

Background.meaning: Background — a description of prior research or prior methods
Background.example: “The dominant sequence transduction models are based on complex recurrent or convolutional neural networks” (Abstract)

Definition.meaning: Definition — a formal definition of a concept / term / variable
Definition.example: “An attention function can be described as mapping a query and a set of key-value pairs to an output, where the query, keys, values, and output are all vectors.” (Section 3.2 Attention)

MethodStep.meaning: MethodStep — a concrete operation that was performed
MethodStep.example: “We compute the dot products of the query with all keys, divide each by √dk, and apply a softmax function to obtain the weights on the values.” (Section 3.2.1)

Observation.meaning: Observation — a sentence describing "what the experiment showed"
Observation.example: “While single-head attention is 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting, quality also drops off with too many heads.” (Section 6.2)

Attribution.meaning: Attribution — a sentence explaining "why a phenomenon happens" (usually contains because / due to / this suggests)
Attribution.example: “This suggests that determining compatibility is not easy and that a more sophisticated compatibility function than dot product may be beneficial.” (Section 6.2)

Concession.meaning: Concession — admitting a flaw / limitation / cost of one's own method
Concession.example: “...at the cost of reduced effective resolution due to averaging attention-weighted positions...” (Section 2)

Compensation.meaning: Compensation — providing a way to make up for the flaw above
Compensation.example: “...an effect we counteract with Multi-Head Attention as described in section 3.2.” (Section 2, following the Concession)

Specific.meaning: Specific — a detailed description of a particular case
Specific.example: “In Table 3 rows (A), we vary the number of attention heads and the attention key and value dimensions, keeping the amount of computation constant” (Section 6.2)

Generalization.meaning: Generalization — extending a specific case into a general conclusion
Generalization.example: “We show that the Transformer generalizes well to other tasks by applying it successfully to English constituency parsing” (Abstract)

Restatement.meaning: Restatement — repeating a claim or conclusion mentioned earlier (usually in the Conclusion)
Restatement.example: “In this work, we presented the Transformer, the first sequence transduction model based entirely on attention” (Conclusion, restating the Abstract's claim)

MetaDiscourse.meaning: MetaDiscourse — guiding language about the paper's structure ("next we will discuss...", "we discuss this in Section X")
MetaDiscourse.example: “In the following sections, we will describe the Transformer, motivate self-attention and discuss its advantages over models such as [17, 18] and [9].” (end of Section 2)

Other.meaning: Other — rhetorical units not belonging to the 14 types above

Elaboration.meaning: Elaboration — the satellite elaborates on the nucleus's content (gives more detail)
Elaboration.example: Nucleus: “We propose a new simple network architecture, the Transformer” / Satellite: “based solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely” (Abstract — the latter elaborates the former)

Background.meaning: Background — the satellite provides the temporal / knowledge background for the nucleus
Background.example: Satellite: “Recurrent neural networks, long short-term memory and gated recurrent neural networks in particular, have been firmly established as state of the art” (start of Intro, setting up the later critique of RNNs)

Cause.meaning: Cause — the satellite is the cause of the nucleus
Cause.example: Cause: “for large values of dk, the dot products grow large in magnitude” / Effect: “pushing the softmax function into regions where it has extremely small gradients” (Section 3.2.1)

Result.meaning: Result — the satellite is the result of the nucleus (opposite direction from Cause)
Result.example: Action: “we scale the dot products by 1/√dk” / Result: resolves the vanishing-gradient problem from the cause above (Section 3.2.1)

Contrast.meaning: Contrast — the satellite and nucleus are in opposition (two sides)
Contrast.example: Old method vs new method: “The dominant ... models are based on complex RNN/CNN” (satellite) ↔ “We propose the Transformer, based solely on attention” (nucleus) (Abstract)

Concession.meaning: Concession — the satellite concedes something, yet the nucleus still holds
Concession.example: Concession: “at the cost of reduced effective resolution” (satellite) / Nucleus: “In the Transformer this is reduced to a constant number of operations” (Section 2 — there is a cost, but the advantage remains)

Evidence.meaning: Evidence — the satellite provides concrete evidence for the nucleus (not a Cause, but supporting data / citations)
Evidence.example: Claim: “the big transformer model outperforms the best previously reported models” / Evidence: “by more than 2.0 BLEU, establishing a new state-of-the-art BLEU score of 28.4” (Section 6.1)

Justify.meaning: Justify — the satellite provides a reason for the nucleus's "action / choice"
Justify.example: Choice: “We chose the sinusoidal version” / Justify: “because it may allow the model to extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than the ones encountered during training” (Section 3.5)

Motivation.meaning: Motivation — the satellite explains why the problem in the nucleus needs solving (making the reader willing to read on)
Motivation.example: Problem: “inherently sequential nature precludes parallelization” / Motivation: “which becomes critical at longer sequence lengths, as memory constraints limit batching across examples” (Intro)

Solutionhood.meaning: Solutionhood — the satellite is the solution to the problem in the nucleus (strong correspondence)
Solutionhood.example: Problem: “reduced effective resolution due to averaging attention-weighted positions” / Solution: “an effect we counteract with Multi-Head Attention” (Section 2)

Sequence.meaning: Sequence — several sentences chained in temporal order (first / then / finally)
Sequence.example: “We compute the dot products → divide each by √dk → apply a softmax function → obtain the weights on the values” (Section 3.2.1 — algorithm step sequence)

Restatement.meaning: Restatement — the satellite restates the nucleus in a different way
Restatement.example: Abstract: “The Transformer ... based solely on attention mechanisms” ↔ Conclusion: “the first sequence transduction model based entirely on attention” (cross-section restatement)

Summary.meaning: Summary — the satellite condenses several preceding points into one sentence
Summary.example: Start of Conclusion “In this work, we presented the Transformer, the first sequence transduction model based entirely on attention, replacing the recurrent layers most commonly used in encoder-decoder architectures with multi-headed self-attention.” (Section 7 — one sentence summarizing the whole paper)

Condition.meaning: Condition — the satellite states that the nucleus holds "under some condition" (if-then structure)
Condition.example: Condition: “While for small values of dk” / Nucleus: “the two mechanisms perform similarly” (Section 3.2.1)

Other.meaning: Other — rhetorical relations not belonging to the 14 types above
Other.example: Inter-sentence relations in footnotes, acknowledgements, copyright notices, etc.

rds.p1: Four tables, non-overlapping — metadata, analysis result, cost log, human judgments. Design principle: structural semantics go to Neo4j, transactional/evaluation data go to SQLite.

rules.listHeading: Overview of the 13 rules (with Vaswani 2017 examples)
rules.listIntro: Each rule is explained in three columns: meaning / trigger condition / Vaswani example. REL-04 / REL-08 / REL-12 require cross-section reasoning and are re-run in the cross-section second pass.

REL-01.name: Claim-Evidence
REL-01.meaning: Every claim should be supported by corresponding evidence (quantitative data, citations, experimental results, or logical inference).
REL-01.trigger: An Abstract / Intro / Results / Discussion section has a Claim FRU, but no nearby Evidence FRU in the same section supports it.
REL-01.example: The Intro writes "the Transformer allows significantly more parallelization and reaches SOTA in 12 hours" — a big claim, but the evidence (Table 2 BLEU scores) only appears in Section 6, with no evidence attached within the Intro paragraph.

REL-02.name: Baseline-Critique
REL-02.meaning: When a baseline is mentioned for comparison, its limitations or shortcomings should be critiqued, not just listed as numbers.
REL-02.trigger: A Method / Experiment section mentions a baseline Entity, but no FRU critiques its limitations.
REL-02.example: Section 6.1 Table 2 lists the BLEU scores of baselines like ByteNet / GNMT / ConvS2S, but does not explain why these baselines lose (what their design limitations are).

REL-03.name: Action-Justification
REL-03.meaning: Every key research action (choosing a dataset / metric / architecture) should have a justification.
REL-03.trigger: A Method section has a MethodStep FRU, but no nearby Motivation FRU explains why it was done that way.
REL-03.example: Section 5.3 writes "we used the Adam optimizer with β1=0.9, β2=0.98" — why Adam over SGD? The paper gives the parameters but not the reason for the choice.

REL-04.name: Macro-Decomposition
REL-04.meaning: The paper as a whole should have a clear macro-structural decomposition — a big problem split into sub-problems, sub-problems split into sub-methods.
REL-04.trigger: Cross-section — the Intro raises several sub-problems, but the Method has no clear mapping to corresponding sub-methods.
REL-04.example: The Intro raises two sub-problems, (1) difficulty of parallelization and (2) long-range dependencies, but the Method never explicitly states a correspondence like "Multi-Head solves problem 1, Self-Attention solves problem 2".

REL-05.name: Process-Sequence
REL-05.meaning: Steps in the Method section should have a clear temporal order, expressed with appropriate connectives or numbering.
REL-05.trigger: The step order in the Method section is unclear (no first/then/finally or numbering).
REL-05.example: Section 3 Model Architecture unfolds clearly with numbering 3.1 / 3.2 / 3.3 / 3.4 / 3.5 (Encoder → Decoder → Attention → FFN → Embedding → Positional) — a healthy example, does not fire.

REL-06.name: Concept-Formalization
REL-06.meaning: A newly introduced concept / term / variable should be formally defined (mathematical definition, operational definition, or formula), not just an analogy or vague description.
REL-06.trigger: An Entity is used but no nearby Definition FRU gives a formal definition.
REL-06.example: The Abstract writes "more parallelizable" without a mathematical definition (what does parallel mean? It is only defined in Section 4 Table 1 via the Sequential Operations column).

REL-07.name: Setup-Scoping
REL-07.meaning: The experiment section should state the scope of the experimental setup (dataset / evaluation metrics / hardware / hyperparameters).
REL-07.trigger: The Experiment section lacks a complete statement of setup scope.
REL-07.example: Section 5 fully lists the dataset (WMT 2014), batch size (25K tokens), hardware (8 P100 GPUs), step time (0.4s), and training time (12 hours) — a healthy example, does not fire.

REL-08.name: Problem-Solution
REL-08.meaning: The problem raised in the Intro should have a corresponding solution described in the Method.
REL-08.trigger: Cross-section — the Intro mentions a problem but the Method gives a solution directly without restating that problem.
REL-08.example: The Intro mentions the problem that "averaging attention-weighted positions reduces resolution"; the Method gives the Multi-Head Attention solution directly but does not restate "the resolution-reduction problem is exactly what we are solving".

REL-09.name: Observation-Attribution
REL-09.meaning: After observing an experimental phenomenon (Observation), an attribution should explain why it happens.
REL-09.trigger: A Results / Discussion section has an Observation FRU, but no Attribution FRU within the nearby [-3, +8] EDU range.
REL-09.example: Section 6.2 Table 3 row (A) writes "too many heads also degrades quality" but offers no explanation at all. In contrast, row (B) has "This suggests that determining compatibility is not easy" right next to it — one attribution sentence makes a big difference.

REL-10.name: Concession-Compensation
REL-10.meaning: When admitting a flaw / limitation of one's own method (Concession), a compensation should be given explaining how it is made up for.
REL-10.trigger: There is a Concession FRU but no nearby Compensation FRU.
REL-10.example: Section 2 mentions "the Transformer's use of attention-weighted positions reduces resolution" as a concession, and the author immediately adds "we compensate with Multi-Head Attention" — a healthy example; the compensation is in place, so it does not fire.

REL-11.name: Specific-Generalization
REL-11.meaning: Specific cases (Specific) and generalized conclusions (Generalization) should be balanced — not examples without conclusions, nor conclusions without examples.
REL-11.trigger: The ratio of Specific FRUs to Generalization FRUs is imbalanced.
REL-11.example: The Abstract writes "the Transformer generalizes well to other tasks" — a strong generalization claim — but only one other task is tested (English constituency parsing); the generalization claim is too strong relative to the specific cases.

REL-12.name: Core-Restatement
REL-12.meaning: The conclusion section should restate the core claims raised in the abstract / introduction, without going off-topic or omitting them.
REL-12.trigger: Cross-section — a claim emphasized in the Abstract is not restated in the Conclusion.
REL-12.example: The Abstract emphasizes "the Transformer generalizes well" (including constituency parsing) but the Conclusion mainly reviews the translation SOTA and does not restate the parsing result — a slight misalignment between Abstract and Conclusion on the generalization claim.

REL-13.name: Meta-Discourse
REL-13.meaning: There should be appropriate meta-discourse between sections — e.g. guiding language like "In the following sections, we will...".
REL-13.trigger: Sections lack guiding / transition language, making it hard for the reader to follow the line of argument.
REL-13.example: The end of Section 2 writes "In the following sections, we will describe the Transformer, motivate self-attention..." — perfect meta-discourse that previews for the reader what comes next. A healthy example.

example.intro: Using one sentence from the Vaswani paper, we trace end-to-end how the system finds a problem. This is an example of REL-09 Observation without Attribution.

step1.title: The original sentence
step1.translation: Plain English gloss: "Single-head attention is 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting; with too many heads, quality also drops."
step1.location: Where it appears: page 9 of the paper, Section 6.2, discussing the experimental result of Table 3 row (A).

step2.title: How the system reads this sentence
step2.intro: The system splits the sentence into a few small propositions (EDUs), then attaches three kinds of sticky notes:
step2.observation: (Observation FRU): "This sentence is 'describing what the experiment showed'."
step2.rst: (RST): "This sentence has a Result causal relation with the Table 3 data."
step2.key: Key point: **no "attribution" sticky note is attached** (Attribution FRU) — because the original text really does not explain why.

step3.title: REL-09 starts working
step3.intro: The rule logic looks at just one thing:
step3.quote: "Next to this observation sentence (within the range of 3 sentences before to 8 sentences after), is there an 'attribution' sticky note attached?"
step3.body: The system looked around this sentence — and found no attribution sticky note at all. So it lists the sentence as a "suspect candidate", ready to hand to the LLM for confirmation.
step3.contrast: Contrast: Section 6.2 row (B) discusses "reducing dk hurts quality" and is immediately followed by "This suggests that determining compatibility is not easy" — that is an "attribution" sticky note, so row (B) is not listed as a candidate.

step4.title: The LLM makes the final verdict
step4.intro: The system hands this candidate to Claude and asks "is this really a defect?" After reading the original text + nearby paragraphs, the LLM replies:
step4.severity: (does not break the core argument but weakens persuasiveness)
step4.confidence: (fairly sure, but with some doubt that the author may have abbreviated intentionally)
step4.suggestion: : "Too many heads make each head's dimension too small (dk = dmodel / h), reducing attention's expressiveness."

step5.title: What the user sees
step5.body: The author observed that "too many heads reduce quality" but did not explain why. The reader only sees the phenomenon, not the cause.
step5.suggestion: Add an attribution along the lines of "with too many heads each head's dimension becomes too small (dk = dmodel / h), making attention's expressiveness insufficient".
step5.footnote: Click this defect card → the PDF viewer automatically scrolls to that paragraph and highlights the original sentence.

step6.title: Advisor judgment → quantify system quality
step6.body1Prefix: After seeing this defect, the advisor can press one of three buttons:
step6.body1Suffix: . The judgment is saved to SQLite.
step6.body2Prefix: These judgments are used to compute the soft precision of each rule (correct + 0.5 × partial), and can also be exported as ground truth.
step6.body2Bold: Judgments are used only for evaluation and analysis; they are never written back into the prompt to influence subsequent adjudication
step6.body2Suffix: , so every check is an independent zero-shot and the result is reproducible.

phase2.p1Prefix: After the system finishes adjudicating, the advisor performs a manual inspection of each defect (correct / partial / wrong) to quantify system quality. The judgment data is used only for evaluation and for exporting ground truth;
phase2.p1Bold: it is never fed back into the prompt
phase2.p1Suffix: — every check is an independent zero-shot and the result is reproducible.
phase2.p2: Human judgments provide a quantitative metric (per-rule soft precision = (correct + 0.5 × partial) / number judged), which can serve as the paper's evaluation result and ground truth, evidencing rule quality.

guards.p1: A floating drawer in the bottom-right corner, restricted to discussing this paper. Four layers of safety:
guards.scope: — can only discuss this paper; declines other topics and steers back to the paper
guards.citeSuffix: , which the frontend parses into clickable chips
guards.injection: — 8 patterns (e.g. "ignore previous instructions", "you are now X", "system:"); when matched, a warning is added to the system prompt
guards.rate: — 15 times per paper per minute (in-memory bucket)

literature.p1: Every layer of the system's design maps to a heavily-cited paper:

perf.p1Prefix: Analyzing a normal paper dispatches about
perf.p1Mid: (3 per section: EDU / ER / RST·FRU; 1 each for the 13 REL rules; 1 cross-section). These calls originally ran serially "one after another"; token-dense Chinese paragraphs take 4–10 seconds each, so a full analysis often took
perf.p1Suffix: . The three changes below compress it to about 1/5.
perf.h1: 11.1 Bottleneck diagnosis (using real data, not guessing)
perf.h1p: The system records the stage, model, tokens, and time of every LLM call into SQLite (the {table} table). Breaking down a real run of the same paper, the time is split almost evenly between two blocks, and each is internally serial:
perf.h2p: Sections are independent of each other, and the 13 rules are also independent of each other, so a capped thread pool dispatches them simultaneously ({maxWorkers}, default 6). Why use threads instead of switching to async: these are all I/O-bound API waits, the OpenAI client is synchronous, so a thread pool is sufficient and minimally invasive.

h2li.crossSection: : each section's EDU→ER→RST·FRU three steps still have ordering dependencies (ER and RST both consume EDU), so it stays serial within a section; only across sections is it parallel.
h2li.crossRule: : the 13 rules run as one parallel batch — this is the single biggest gain.
h2li.safe: : SQLite opens a new connection per call + WAL mode, Neo4j opens a new session per call (the driver itself is thread-safe), Neo4j writes happen only after the parallel section; {poolMap} preserves input order, so result assembly is deterministic.
h2li.ratePrefix: : the pool is capped to avoid hammering OpenAI's rate limit, and the underlying
h2li.rateSuffix: already has built-in exponential backoff retries for 429/5xx.

perf.h3: 11.3 Output slimming: only write a reason when it "really violates"
perf.h3p1Prefix: Rule checking originally required the LLM to return severity / section / description / suggestion and other fields for
perf.h3p1Suffix: candidate — but the system actually keeps only the violating ones and discards the rest. For rules with many candidates, this amounts to forcing the model to write a lot of Chinese and then throwing it away. For example, REL-06 (Concept-Formalization) has 60–70 candidates in one paper with only 5 violations, yet spat out ~7000 output tokens and took ~100 seconds.
perf.h3p2Suffix: , detail fields filled in only when violating". The defect results are completely unchanged (non-violations were discarded anyway), but REL-06 went from 7069 → 1554 tokens, 101s → 20s.
perf.h5p: Some LaTeX papers use fonts without a ToUnicode CMap, so copying/extracting produces garbled text ({garbled} is actually {chapter}). After native extraction the system runs a lightweight detection (looking at the proportion of noise characters such as backticks/asterisks), and if it judges the text garbled it automatically falls back to tesseract OCR (Traditional Chinese + English), preserving the page number and bbox coordinates of each text segment. Text extraction was moved into a background task, so OCR (~3–5 minutes for 30 pages) does not block the upload request.
perf.h6p: These refactors changed a fair amount of orchestration logic, so a set of millisecond-level unit tests that touch no network/LLM/Neo4j ({tests}) were added: garbled detection (real garbled samples, clean Chinese/English, text heavy in statistical symbols to prevent false positives) and the native→OCR routing (mocking out the extractor to test only the decision). The garbled-detection path had had a bug before, and the tests verified via "red → green" that they really catch that bug.
